candidate_concepts.label: McCulloch-Pitts neuron model
candidate_concepts.description: The first computational model of a neuron, proposed by Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts in 1943, representing neurons as simple electrical circuits.
coverage_criteria: Identify McCulloch and Pitts as the authors of the first neuron model in 1943.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video clearly states that the first step towards neural networks was in 1943 when McCulloch and Pitts wrote a paper on how neurons might work and modeled a simple neural network with electrical circuits.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This candidate captures a single historical milestone without combining with later developments, making it checkable with a single identification question.

candidate_concepts.label: Hebbian learning
candidate_concepts.description: The principle that neural pathways are strengthened each time they are used, introduced by Donald Hebb in his 1949 book 'The Organization of Behavior'.
coverage_criteria: State that Hebbian learning means neural pathways strengthen with use.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video mentions Hebb's book and the key idea that neural pathways are strengthened each time they are used.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a distinct and foundational learning rule that can be assessed independently without requiring details from other milestones.

candidate_concepts.label: Rosenblatt's Perceptron
candidate_concepts.description: A single-layer neural network model that computes a weighted sum of inputs, subtracts a threshold, and outputs one of two classes; built in hardware and the oldest neural network still in use.
coverage_criteria: Explain how the perceptron performs binary classification using weighted sum and threshold.
Identify Rosenblatt as the creator of the perceptron in 1958.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video provides a detailed description of the perceptron: it computes a weighted sum, subtracts a threshold, and outputs one of two values; it is the oldest NN still in use.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: The perceptron is a core concept in neural networks, and focusing on its mechanism (weighted sum, threshold, binary output) allows assessment of fundamental understanding without overcomplicating with later variants.

candidate_concepts.label: ADALINE and MADALINE
candidate_concepts.description: Early adaptive linear neural network models (Multiple Adaptive Linear Elements) developed by Bernard Widrow and Marcian Hoff; MADALINE was the first neural network applied to a real-world problem (echo cancellation) and remains in commercial use.
coverage_criteria: Name ADALINE and MADALINE as early neural networks that used adaptive linear elements.
Identify echo cancellation as the real-world application of MADALINE.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source explicitly states that ADALINE and MADALINE were named for their use of multiple adaptive linear elements, that MADALINE was the first applied to a real-world problem, and that it is still in commercial use for eliminating echoes on phone lines.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This candidate highlights an important step toward practical neural networks, distinct from the perceptron, and can be checked by asking about the name expansion and application.

candidate_concepts.label: Minsky & Papert critique and AI winter
candidate_concepts.description: The 1969 book 'Perceptrons' by Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert proved the limitations of perceptrons, leading to a halt in neural network funding and research until 1981.
coverage_criteria: Explain that Minsky and Papert's work demonstrated limitations of perceptrons, causing a decline in neural network research.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video states that Minsky and Papert proved the perceptron to be limited, and progress halted due to fear and unfulfilled claims, causing a funding halt until 1981.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This event is a distinct turning point in neural network history, and its impact can be assessed through a single question about the cause and effect of the research slowdown.

candidate_concepts.label: Hopfield networks and the revival of neural network research
candidate_concepts.description: John Hopfield's 1982 paper to the National Academy of Sciences, combined with the US-Japan Conference on Cooperative Competitive Neural Networks, rekindled interest and funding in neural networks after the AI winter.
coverage_criteria: State that Hopfield's 1982 approach and the US-Japan conference helped restart neural network funding.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video describes Hopfield's likable and charismatic approach, and the US-Japan conference where Japan announced their fifth-generation effort, leading to renewed US funding.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This candidate captures the revival trigger, distinct from the earlier decline, and can be assessed with a simple recall of the key figures and event.

name_drops: US-Japan Conference on Cooperative Competitive Neural Networks

candidate_concepts.label: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)
candidate_concepts.description: A recurrent neural network framework proposed in 1997 by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, designed to address long-term dependencies in sequences. (Source misspells names as Schimberger and Hochreicher.)
coverage_criteria: Identify LSTM as a recurrent neural network framework proposed in 1997.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video states that a recurrent neural network framework, LSTM, was proposed by [Schimberger and Hochreicher] in 1997. (The actual authors are Hochreiter and Schmidhuber; we note the discrepancy.)
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: LSTM is a specific advanced architecture in deep learning, and this candidate isolates its historical introduction without delving into its technical details, making it checkable.

candidate_concepts.label: Gradient-based learning for document recognition
candidate_concepts.description: Yann LeCun's 1998 paper 'Gradient-based learning applied to document recognition' advanced the application of gradient-based learning methods, notably in convolutional neural networks for document analysis.
coverage_criteria: Identify Yann LeCun's 1998 publication on gradient-based learning for document recognition.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source mentions LeCun's publication as a significant step in the timeline.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This candidate highlights a key paper that influenced modern deep learning, and can be assessed by a single recall.

name_drops: Gradient-based learning applied to document recognition
